nodes.description: The respiratory-chain deficit produced by defective mitochondrial translation is not uniform. Complex I, whose subunits are the most dependent on mtDNA-encoded synthesis, is disproportionately affected, and the pattern of deficiency differs between cell types derived from the same patient. In differentiated neurons, complex I specifically is sequestered into PINK1/Parkin-positive autophagosomes, so active mitophagy - not only failed assembly - contributes to the neuronal deficit. This is the mechanistic reason why one heteroplasmic variant produces a neuron-weighted, rather than uniformly systemic, disease.

nodes.description: Retinal dystrophy is an ocular source of visual loss distinct from cortical visual impairment. In a 29-person m.3243A>G carrier cohort, four grades ranged from fine pigment changes visible on autofluorescence, through macular pigment deposits, to extrafoveal chorioretinal atrophy and finally foveal atrophy with marked visual-acuity loss. Retinal abnormalities affected 25 carriers; this is not a MELAS-specific prevalence estimate. Grade correlated with age and visual acuity, without an observed correlation with heteroplasmy or overall disease involvement. Variable or absent systemic features can obscure recognition of the mitochondrial retinal disorder.

Two patients (7%) with retinal abnormalities had grade 4 disease, in which the fovea was affected by atrophy, with marked loss of visual acuity.

nodes.description: The pathogenic MT-TL1 variants abolish the normal taurine-containing modification (5-taurinomethyluridine) at the anticodon wobble position of mitochondrial tRNA-Leu(UUR). The same defect is the rationale for taurine supplementation.

nodes.description: Induced pluripotent stem cells reprogrammed from m.3243A>G patients, then differentiated to neurons and to teratoma-derived tissues. The model exists because the mitochondrial genome cannot be edited by transgenic methods, so patient cells are the only route to a human m.3243A>G system. Its distinctive result is that respiratory-chain deficiency is cell-type specific from one shared genotype, with complex I predominating as it does in patient tissue, and that neurons additionally clear complex I by mitophagy.
